records.place: Sauternes, on the left bank of the Garonne, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château d'Yquem
wine.classification: Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification, a rank held by no other estate
wine.grapes: Sémillon, about three quarters, with Sauvignon Blanc for the rest.
wine.sites: A hill above the village of Sauternes, gravel and sand over clay, where autumn mists from the cold Ciron and the warmer Garonne bring the noble rot.
wine.making: Pickers pass through the vines many times over several weeks, taking only berries shrivelled by noble rot. Each day's pick is pressed and fermented in new oak barrels, raised in barrel for well over a year, blended and bottled at the château; in a year judged too poor, nothing is released under the name.
wine.glass: Apricot, saffron, barley sugar and orange marmalade over pineapple, vanilla and crème brûlée; luscious and deep, yet carried by fresh acidity to a long finish of honey and bitter orange peel.
wine.ageing: Delicious from release, it deepens to amber over decades and can last a century in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, an old bottle a degree or two warmer; no need to decant a young bottle; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of five communes on the Ciron; by law its wine is sweet.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Ranked alone above every other sweet wine in 1855, Château d'Yquem is mostly Sémillon, picked berry by berry over many passes as noble rot takes hold. It tastes of apricot, saffron and marmalade, and can last a century.
records.story: In 1593 the Sauvage family, local nobles, took the tenure of Yquem, and over the next two centuries they made the hill above Sauternes their own. In 1785 the Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family; widowed three years later, she ran the estate herself through the Revolution. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), touring Bordeaux as the American minister in Paris, ordered Yquem for himself and, the story goes, for George Washington. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers set Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, a rank made for it and never shared. The Lur-Saluces family kept the estate for more than two centuries and kept its discipline: many passes through the vines for each harvest, and no wine at all under the name in years judged too poor, among them 1964, 1972, 1974 and 1992. In 1959 they added a dry white, Y, sold as Bordeaux. After a long family dispute the estate passed in 1999 to the luxury group LVMH, and Yquem again declined a vintage in 2012. Guests ask for it by name, and it needs no partner at all, though foie gras and Roquefort are its classic companions.

others.name: Y du Château d'Yquem
others.note: The dry white of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, sold as Bordeaux and never as Sauternes; a different wine, not a second wine.

traps: Premier Cru Supérieur is Yquem's alone; the eleven estates below it are Premiers Crus.
Y is a dry wine sold as Bordeaux, not Sauternes, and it is not a second wine of Yquem.
Yquem releases nothing under its name in a year it judges too poor, so a missing vintage is a decision, not a lost bottle.

cards.front: Château d'Yquem: what rank did the 1855 classification give it?
cards.back: Premier Cru Supérieur, a rank made for it alone, above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac.

cards.front: In which years did Château d'Yquem release no wine under its name?
cards.back: Years judged too poor, among them 1964, 1972, 1974, 1992 and 2012.

questions.q: A guest asks how Château d'Yquem gathers grapes for its sweet wine. Which answer fits?
opts: Many passes through the vines for nobly rotten berries
One early pick of sound, ripe bunches
Frozen grapes picked on a winter night
Grapes dried on straw mats after harvest
questions.exp: Pickers pass through Yquem's vines many times, taking only berries shrivelled by noble rot; frozen grapes make ice wine and straw mats make vin de paille.

questions.q: From a marriage of 1785 until 1999, which family held Château d'Yquem?
questions.exp: The Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family in 1785, and they held Yquem until 1999; the Sauvages held it before, and the Ségurs held Lafite and Latour.

records.place: Barsac, in the Sauternes district, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château Climens
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon alone, with no Sauvignon Blanc at all.
wine.sites: One block on the Barsac plateau, on the commune's higher ground: red sand and gravel over limestone, the stony subsoil keeping the wine fresh.
wine.making: Picked in several passes for nobly rotten berries, each pass and each parcel is fermented apart in oak barrels, a part of them new. The lots are raised in barrel for well over a year, and the blend is made late, from the lots that show the estate's freshness, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Lemon curd, quince and candied ginger over acacia honey, white peach and a little saffron; sweet but airy, with bright acidity running through it and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its freshness, it gains honey and dried apricot over twenty years and keeps for decades after.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The commune's own appellation; a Barsac estate may print Barsac or Sauternes, and Climens prints Barsac.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant.

records.table: Made from Sémillon alone on red sand over limestone, Château Climens is the Barsac Premier Cru its admirers call the Lord of Barsac. Sweet yet light on its feet, it tastes of lemon curd, quince and candied ginger.
records.story: Climens lies on the Barsac plateau, where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and the autumn mists that follow bring noble rot to the grapes. Barsac's soils are thin over limestone, and its wines are known for tension rather than weight; Climens, on the commune's higher ground of red sand, became the clearest example. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked it among the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, beneath Yquem alone. In 1971 it was bought by a Bordeaux family that already held several growths of the Médoc, and from 1992 a daughter of that family ran it for some thirty years. She kept the vineyard to Sémillon alone, picked in many passes, and kept each pass and each parcel apart in barrel until a late blend, so that the freshness of the finished wine was chosen rather than left to chance; in the 2010s she turned the farming to biodynamics. In 2022 the family sold the estate. Through each change of hands Climens has held to one idea: that Barsac's limestone and Sémillon alone can make a sweet wine that feels weightless. Its lesson for a candidate is simple: Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac, never required.

others.name: Cyprès de Climens
others.note: The second wine, Sémillon from the same plateau, lighter and ready sooner.

traps: A Barsac estate may label its wine Barsac or Sauternes; an estate elsewhere in Sauternes may not use Barsac.
Climens is Sémillon alone: do not describe it as a Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc blend.

cards.front: Château Climens: what grape, and on what soil?
cards.back: Sémillon alone, on red sand and gravel over the limestone of the Barsac plateau.

cards.front: What two names may a Barsac estate such as Climens print on its label?
cards.back: Barsac or Sauternes; an estate in the other four communes may use only Sauternes.

questions.q: A guest asks how much Sauvignon Blanc goes into Château Climens. What do you answer?
opts: About a quarter, as at Yquem
Half, with Sémillon for the rest
Most of it, with a little Muscadelle
questions.exp: Climens is planted to Sémillon alone, which shows that Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac but never required; a quarter is close to Yquem's share.

questions.q: In 1971 Château Climens was bought by owners who held it for half a century. Who were they?
questions.exp: The Lurton family, owners of several Médoc growths, bought Climens in 1971 and sold it in 2022; AXA bought Suduiraut in 1992, and LVMH took Yquem in 1999.

records.place: Barsac, in the Sauternes district, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château Coutet
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon, the great majority, with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle.
wine.sites: One block around the château and its tower on the Barsac plateau, thin clay and sand over the limestone that runs close beneath the commune.
wine.making: Picked in several passes for nobly rotten berries, it is fermented in oak barrels, many of them new, and raised in barrel for well over a year before bottling at the château. In rare years a small selection of Sémillon, the ripest lots of the vintage, is bottled apart as Cuvée Madame.
wine.glass: Lime, grapefruit and acacia over apricot, honeysuckle and a little beeswax; sweet but taut, with lively acidity and a long, clean finish of candied lemon.
wine.ageing: Bright and appealing in its first five years, it gains honey and marmalade with age and keeps for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; serve it straight from the bottle, with no decanting; a small tulip glass.

label.means: The commune appellation Coutet uses; Barsac wine may also be sold as Sauternes.
Bottled at the estate, whose cellars run beneath the tower.

records.table: Around a tower of the thirteenth century on the Barsac plateau grows Château Coutet, mostly Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc. Sweet but taut, lime and apricot over limestone, it bottles a richer selection, Cuvée Madame, only in exceptional years.
records.story: Aquitaine belonged to the English crown when the square tower at the heart of Coutet was raised in the thirteenth century, and the estate grew around it on the Barsac plateau. From the late eighteenth century Coutet belonged to the Lur-Saluces family, who also held Yquem, and it stayed with them for well over a hundred years. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Coutet a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac, beside its neighbour Climens, the two Barsac estates of that rank. In the twentieth century it passed through other hands, and its rare selection, Cuvée Madame, from the ripest Sémillon of exceptional years, made the estate's name among collectors. In 1977 the Baly family bought Coutet and set about restoring the vineyard, the cellars and the old buildings. They kept the Barsac style that the plateau gives: sweet wine with the tension of limestone, less broad than the Sauternes of the hills, and in the years of plenty they set aside the few barrels of Cuvée Madame. Coutet makes the case for Barsac's own appellation, and for the right of a Barsac estate to print Sauternes instead if it wishes.

others.name: Cuvée Madame
others.note: A rare selection of the estate's ripest Sémillon, made only in exceptional years.

others.name: La Chartreuse de Coutet
others.note: The second wine, sweet Barsac ready sooner.

others.name: Opalie de Château Coutet
others.note: A dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux.

traps: Barsac is one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes appellation, and it also has its own.
Cuvée Madame is not made every year, and it is a separate selection, not the estate's standard wine.

cards.front: Château Coutet: what is Cuvée Madame?
cards.back: A rare selection of the estate's ripest Sémillon, bottled apart only in exceptional years.

cards.front: Which Barsac Premier Cru grows around a square tower of the thirteenth century?

questions.q: A guest wants a Barsac Premier Cru that blends in a little Muscadelle, unlike its all Sémillon neighbour. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Coutet blends Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle; Climens next door is Sémillon alone, and Yquem and Gilette are not in Barsac.

questions.q: In 1977 a new family bought Château Coutet and restored its vineyard and cellars. Which family?
questions.exp: The Baly family bought Coutet in 1977; the Lurtons bought Climens in 1971, the Médevilles are Gilette's family and the Moueix are Libourne merchants.

records.place: Preignac, in the Sauternes district, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château Suduiraut
wine.classification: Premier Cru in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac
wine.grapes: Sémillon, the great majority, with Sauvignon Blanc for the rest.
wine.sites: A broad estate in Preignac whose vines run to the edge of Yquem's, sand and gravel over clay, where the Ciron's morning mists hang late into the autumn.
wine.making: Picked in many passes for nobly rotten berries, each pass is fermented apart in oak barrels, a part of them new, and raised in barrel for well over a year. The passes are blended only at the end, and the wine is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, roasted pineapple and honey over saffron, vanilla and orange peel; rich and broad, with an oily texture held up by acidity and a long, sweet finish of marmalade.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy young, it turns to amber, marmalade and toffee over twenty to thirty years and lasts far longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; decanting is not needed; a white wine glass, filled no more than a third.

label.means: The appellation of five communes on the Ciron, Preignac among them; its wine is sweet by law.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant.

records.table: Pour Château Suduiraut for the rich side of Sauternes: Sémillon led, from Preignac vines that run to the edge of Yquem's. Expect candied apricot, roasted pineapple and honey on an oily texture, beside foie gras or a blue cheese.
records.story: Formal gardens in the French manner, attributed by tradition to André Le Nôtre (1613 to 1700), the gardener of Versailles, frame the house at Suduiraut. The estate carries the name of the Suduiraut family, its owners in the seventeenth century, whose house, the story goes, was burnt during the Fronde, the civil wars of the 1650s, and rebuilt in the decades after. The vineyard climbs the low hills of Preignac to the border of Yquem, and the Ciron's mists that settle there bring noble rot in most autumns. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Suduiraut a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac. Through the twentieth century it passed between private owners until 1992, when it was bought by AXA Millésimes, the wine estates of the French insurance group, which had taken Pichon Baron in Pauillac in 1987. The new owners kept the house style, broad Sémillon picked late in many passes, and added a dry white under the letter S, as Rieussec has its R and Guiraud its G, so that sound grapes from years with little rot find a use. Set beside Climens or Coutet, Suduiraut gives the other face of the district: Preignac's breadth against the tension of Barsac across the Ciron.

others.name: Castelnau de Suduiraut
others.note: The second wine, Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from the same estate.

others.name: S de Suduiraut
others.note: A dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux because Sauternes must be sweet.

traps: The five Sauternes communes are Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac; Suduiraut is in Preignac.
Suduiraut is a Premier Cru, not a Premier Cru Supérieur: that rank is Yquem's alone.
S de Suduiraut is dry and sold as Bordeaux; it is not the estate's sweet wine.

cards.front: Château Suduiraut: which famous neighbour do its vines border?
cards.back: Château d'Yquem, across the line between Preignac and Sauternes.

cards.front: What is S de Suduiraut, and why is it not labelled Sauternes?
cards.back: The estate's dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc; the Sauternes appellation is for sweet wine, so it is sold as Bordeaux.

questions.q: A guest wants the rich, broad side of Sauternes rather than the tension of Barsac. Which Premier Cru fits?
questions.exp: Suduiraut, in Preignac, is rich and oily, apricot and pineapple; Climens and Coutet are the taut Barsac pair, and Y is a dry wine.

questions.q: In 1992 Château Suduiraut was bought by the wine estates of a French group. Which group?
opts: The bank of the Rothschild family
questions.exp: AXA Millésimes bought Suduiraut in 1992, five years after Pichon Baron; LVMH took Yquem in 1999.

records.place: Preignac, in the Sauternes district, Bordeaux

wine.name: Château Gilette Crème de Tête
wine.grapes: Mainly Sémillon, with a little Sauvignon Blanc.
wine.sites: A small vineyard in the commune of Preignac, picked in passes for nobly rotten berries like the classed growths around it.
wine.making: Fermented without oak, the wine is put into small concrete vats filled to the brim, so that little air reaches it, and kept there for many years, often close to twenty, before it is bottled. It then rests again in the cellar and is released only when the family judges it ready.
wine.glass: Crème brûlée, dried apricot and orange marmalade over toffee, quince paste and a little coffee; deep, mellow and long, with a freshness the years in sealed vats have kept.
wine.ageing: Released already mature, decades after the harvest, it is ready to drink and holds for many years more in bottle.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, an old bottle a degree or two warmer; decant gently only if a crust has formed; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The estate's first selection, made only in the years rich enough for it.
The appellation; Gilette was not ranked in 1855 and prints no classification.

records.table: Kept for many years in concrete vats and never in oak, Château Gilette's Crème de Tête reaches the list already mature. The small Preignac estate stood outside the 1855 list, and its wine tastes of crème brûlée and dried apricot, fresh even after decades.
records.story: When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification of the sweet wines in 1855, Gilette, in Preignac, one of the five communes of Sauternes, was not among the estates ranked, and since that list has never been reopened it has stayed outside it. The appellation decree of 1936 gave it the same Sauternes name as Yquem, and what has made Gilette known is not rank but time. For generations the estate was worked by the Médeville family, growers of Preignac, and their way of raising the wine is what sets it apart. After fermentation the wine goes not into barrels but into small concrete vats, filled to the brim so that little air reaches it, and there it rests for many years, often close to twenty, before it is bottled. It then waits again in the cellar, so that a Gilette reaches a list already decades old. The great years become Crème de Tête; lesser years are bottled under plainer labels. The result is a Sauternes aged without oak and without the breath of a barrel: deep and mellow, yet with a freshness that surprises a guest who reads the vintage. For a sommelier it is the rare chance to offer mature Sauternes without a cellar of one's own.

others.name: Château Les Justices
others.note: The Médeville family's other Sauternes, raised in the usual way and released young; a separate wine, not a second wine of Gilette.

traps: Gilette was not ranked in 1855; it is not a Premier Cru, whatever its reputation.
A Gilette on release is already decades old, so an old vintage on the list is no sign of a forgotten bottle.
Crème de Tête is aged in concrete vats, not in oak barrels.

cards.front: Château Gilette Crème de Tête: in what vessels is it aged, and for how long?
cards.back: Small concrete vats, never oak, for many years, often close to twenty, before it is bottled and released.

cards.front: Was Château Gilette ranked in the 1855 classification of Sauternes and Barsac?
cards.back: No: it stood outside the list in 1855 and has stayed outside it, since the list has never been reopened.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that a Gilette Crème de Tête on the list is already decades old. What do you explain?
opts: It is held for years in concrete vats before release
It was a forgotten bottle found in an old cellar
It is a solera blend of many vintages
It was declassified and sold off late
questions.exp: Gilette ages its Crème de Tête for many years in small concrete vats and releases it mature; it is a single vintage, not a solera.

questions.q: Château Gilette was left unranked in 1855. What gave it the Sauternes name it shares with Yquem?
questions.exp: The appellation decree of 1936 gave the estates of the five communes the Sauternes name; the list of 1855 ranked estates but left Gilette out.
